And then it says because there is suspicion that in Pilica between Zvornik and Bijeljina, as a member of the 10th Sabotage Detachment of the army of Republika Srpska, within the armed conflict of the territory of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina, together with seven members of the army of Republika Srpska, he committed killings of the civilian population in the following way: In the period from 1030 until 1600 hours they killed about 1.200 ethnic Muslim citizens by firearms, who had previously been brought by buses to the site of execution, and the person mentioned himself killed about 100 identified persons as he was shooting with an M-70A automatic rifle by individual gunfire and in this way he committed the crime of a war crime against the civilian population from Article 142, paragraph 1 of the Penal Code of Yugoslavia. Is that right, Mr. Erdemovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So just a few days after you set foot on Yugoslav soil, you were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. arrested precisely because of what you had just testified about, and the explanation refers to Gojkovic Branko, Savanovic Stanko, Goronja Zoran, Golijan Vlastimir, Boskic Marko, Kos Franc, and Cvetkovic Aleksandar. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is what you're testifying about here.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is mentioned here is something that you also said, and that is a lieutenant colonel of the army of Republika Srpska unknown to you, and that you went to the village of Pilica, Zvornik, Bijeljinja, and then what is described is roughly what you spoke of here; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know, I hope, that then on the basis of these criminal charges brought against you, the authorities, the judicial authorities in charge, the judicial authorities of Serbia, because the public prosecutor instituted an investigation on the basis of this criminal report, you were sent to custody; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, you don't have this criminal report. It is dated the 6th of March, 1996, and it says that the accused was arrested on the 3rd of March, which means only ten days after he crossed into Serbia. So could this be admitted into evidence as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just let the witness identify it. If you would show it to the witness and then we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I read parts of this report, and the witness confirmed that it was correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, but let him look at it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just have to say that this document was never shown to me and that I didn't sign it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. The next exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 169, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A criminal report is not signed by the person against whom it is issued, but I also have in connection with the question I put to you, since the public prosecutor instituted an investigation, I assume that was given to you, the side opposite has this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, it has the number ERN 00399959, page 1, and then it goes on from there, the following numbers. It is the district public prosecutor's office in Novi Sad, on the 8th of March, 1996. So two days after the criminal report, and here there is a request for the investigation to be conducted against Drazen Erdemovic. And under number 2, against Radoslav Kremenovic. And in this document, again reference is made to the fact that they had killed about 1.200 citizens of Muslim ethnicity with firearms and committed, thereby, a war crime as envisaged by the Criminal Code. Could this be admitted into evidence as well, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The witness has just been shown a copy of the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd get the accused's copy. Mr. Erdemovic, if there is anything you want to say about that document, you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I wish to say is that there are several dates there that are not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. We'll get the next number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 170, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the title of the document, Mr. Milosevic? Or Mr. Erdemovic, you can tell me. The title of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says that this is a request for conducting an investigation against me and a person who was in my unit. He was deputy commander of my unit, and his name is Kremenovic Radoslav.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We have already the English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the normal order; first the criminal report of the police, then the request for conducting an investigation by the public prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, Mr. Erdemovic, you were not tried by Yugoslav courts for this act, but your extradition was requested. You know that. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is how you arrived here and you were put on trial here; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Precisely for the act as it is described in the criminal report and the request for the conduct of an investigation issued by the Yugoslav authorities; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I have been able to see from these documents, you yourself confessed that you personally had killed about 100 men; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the total was about 1.200, according to this report. You said 1.000 a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said between 1.000 and 1.200.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it beyond dispute that for killing more than a thousand men and for personally killing about 100 men you were sentenced to a prison term of five years? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Court has the record. Mr. Nice, perhaps you can assist us. What was the offence for which this accused was ultimately convicted?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's dealt with on paragraph 3, violation of Article 3 of the Statute, violation of the laws and customs of war. I don't, I think, have the indictment with me. If I -- I do. Mr. Waespi forecasting your need for it. I can make the indictment available to you, if you'd like to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we should have a copy of the indictment. It should be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Can I get it copied in sufficient numbers and we'll make it available in a few minutes. Or immediately, as you prefer. I've only got one copy now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll do it in due course. Let's have some copies when there's time to do it. We will have the copies. We will give it the next tab number, I should think, from 514.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 514, tab 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The issue which the Trial Chamber is concerned about, of course, is the way in which it is put. I haven't seen the indictment - no doubt I will have a copy in a moment - but it is for war crimes. No specific numbers are mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think not, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, in the plea arrangement, wouldn't there have been a specific number?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll deal with that, if I may, after the next adjournment, if we get that far, or as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We ought to have it clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Erdemovic, there's no dispute over the fact that you personally killed 100 men and participated in the killing of more than a thousand men.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I never denied the fact that I had done it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As we heard from Mr. Nice, you were charged here for customs of war, not even for murder. Isn't that right, Mr. Erdemovic? Violations of the laws and customs of war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't know if the witness can help us with that, which no doubt depends on a legal technicality. What we will do: We've Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. got the indictment and we'll get the plea agreement in front us as soon as we can so that we have the full --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have the plea agreement with me now. Perhaps you'll just give me a moment to read it myself and then I'll hand it in when it's convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I can continue. That is the whole point, Mr. May, that this is quite absurd, that you are producing a witness here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Don't use words like that. It's quite out of the question. Now, what's your question for the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is so obvious, but I'll come to my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Erdemovic, you signed a plea agreement with this so-called Prosecutor's office; is that right? OTP.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I signed such an agreement which was approved by the Trial Chamber. It was not just an agreement between me and the OTP, and all the Judges had a copy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't doubt that they were informed about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, the Chamber will probably be assisted now rather than later by seeing perhaps paragraphs 11 and 12 of the plea agreement, the document that the accused referred to. And I think this probably encapsulates the overall position of the parties at trial, although the document can be read in full.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment while we read this. Yes. The agreement, which we'll exhibit in a moment, states that the witness acknowledges that he did shoot and kill and did participate with other members of his unit and soldiers from another unit in the shooting and killing of unarmed Bosnian men, and the summary executions resulted in the deaths of hundreds of Bosnian Muslim male civilians, although it's acknowledged that it's not possible on the evidence to determine how many persons he actually killed. I read that for the point of view of the record, but we've heard the witness's evidence in front of us today as to the numbers involved. Yes. We'll get a number for that. Next tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, Prosecution Exhibit 514, tab 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since you have quoted a part of this agreement, I would like to draw attention to a part of the agreement which is headed "Obligations of the Prosecution," and it says that the Prosecution will withdraw the alternative charges from the indictment. That is point 1, crimes against humanity, punishable under 5(A), murder of the Statute of the International Tribunal, and will propose to the Trial Chamber to reject that paragraph when sentencing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Erdemovic, in your agreement this so-called Prosecution, though you said that you had killed more than a hundred men, withdrew the charge of murder. What do you think were the reasons for this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not for him to say. That's for the Prosecution to say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. I think it's up to you too probably, because it is quite unbelievable that you should call such a witness here who, on the basis of an agreement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Confine yourself to questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. I will confine myself to questions, though it's almost superfluous to engage in that exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You even stated that the facts and allegations in paragraphs 1 to 15 of the indictment of the 22nd of May, 1996, would have been proven beyond any reasonable doubt. So you knew what would have been proven, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're talking about. I don't understand. You're just reading a part of something that I cannot understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am talking about this agreement.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: The agreement was made eight years ago, and I now cannot remember all the details of that agreement. I had a lawyer at the time who was present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm quoting from this the agreement, paragraph 7: "Drazen Erdemovic also acknowledges that he realises that he would be found guilty of crimes against humanity, Article 5 (A) of the Statute of the International Tribunal and all the mentioned elements would have been proven beyond any reasonable doubt." So I'm quoting from your own agreement, an agreement that you engaged in with the Prosecution. Is that right or not? You knew what would have been proven and what would have not.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I just know what I said, what happened where, and that the Prosecution had the evidence. They showed them photographs. I had nothing more to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, how much time did you spend in prison altogether for all these acts you were charged with and condemned for?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't even spend a full five years, did you?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No. But that wasn't a decision taken by the Prosecution to release me. In fact, the Prosecution opposed my early release from prison, but the President of the Tribunal, Judge McDonald, decided that I should be released earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Prosecution agreed that for a hundred men killed you be sentenced to a term of five years; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: If that is what it says there, it is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it quite clear to everyone that for such a mass execution you received five years only on condition that you accuse others? Is that right? It's not a problem -- the problem is not your testimony, the problem is the lies.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Lies about what? What?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Saying that this had been done following orders from the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska. That is what you're alleging. What I am alleging and what I know is that in order to organise anything like that, the authorities had to know about it. My unit, we or I, could not have provided all the buses and all these other things. It would be quite clear to anyone that someone very high up was behind it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can get a translation for that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Repeat it, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what was not translated. I asked, "And what was behind this agreement then?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the reason, in your opinion, for you to be forgiven --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. He can't answer that. The witness can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This agreement between this so-called Prosecution and Drazen Erdemovic, has it been admitted as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, I don't have to tender it. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am afraid that something was not quite clear. Maybe the question wasn't translated, that is, whether he always spoke the truth as to who issued the order for this to be done. I think that remained open.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will clarify it. Mr. Erdemovic, have you told us the truth in your evidence today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In particular, have you told us the truth insofar as Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you know it as to who ordered these executions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I always said who gave orders to me. I don't know who gave orders to my officers. I always talked about the commanding officer of my unit and who gave me orders that day on the farm. I never mentioned any other persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again there is no translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, there is now. Yes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. It was my understanding on the basis of what you were saying here today that you were given orders by a member of your unit, Brano Grujic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No, that's not right. His name is Brano Gojkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Gojkovic. All right. I made a mistake when I noted the name. He's a member of your unit; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also claim that he was ordered to do so, as far as I can see from this criminal report, by some unidentified lieutenant colonel of the army of Republika Srpska, and you don't know who he is and where he's from except for the fact that you assume, as far as I can see, that he's from the Drina Corps. That was your explanation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you belong to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: An unidentified lieutenant colonel from the Drina Corps comes and orders you to kill a thousand persons and you carry out that order. Is that what you're trying to say? Can a normal person do that?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I did not say that he came. I said that Brano and Aleksandar Cvetkovic, probably on Pelemis's orders, went and found this lieutenant colonel in Zvornik. He didn't come to see us. Brano Gojkovic and Aleksandar Cvetkovic went to Zvornik to a reception area, and they went out of there with this lieutenant colonel and two military policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. As far as I understand this, the other side justified to the public your five-year sentence by the fact that you had been forced to do certain things; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can't speak for the other side, as you call them, the Prosecution. It's not for him to speak for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had access to the media all the time, access to information too. You could have said when you were arrested in Yugoslavia that you were forced or that you were not forced. I did not notice any of that in these documents that we've exhibited here.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I always said that I had received orders to do so. Had this not been my orders, I never would have harmed anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's just take a look -- let's first clarify a few matters. When you joined the army of Republika Srpska, you reported to the military department in Bijeljina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you were in this 10th Sabotage Detachment and you say that this was a unit that reconnoitred in the territory held by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in certain parts of the territory held by them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnic composition of this unit of yours, this detachment of yours? On the basis of what you've been saying here, it was my understanding that it was a multi-ethnic detachment.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At first when this unit was established, there were only Croats there, one Muslim, and one Slovene. These Croats helped the Serbs to get out of Tuzla, to territory held by the army of Republika Srpska. Afterwards, in October, the unit expanded and then it was joined by Serbs too who came from all parts of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. When we talk about these events, I have in my hands here part of the transcript from your testimony. It doesn't have an ERN number, Mr. May. It says IT-951861, IT-9995861. Mr. Harmon is putting the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It should have a page number. If it's a transcript, it should have a page number. It may be at the top right of the page. You can refer us to that, please. The top right of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, it only says transcript up there because this is a translation into the Serbian language. And I wish to go back to certain things that Mr. Erdemovic alleged here. I just want to quote that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just help us with this. How far is it into the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I have here is page 1, 2, 3 up to -- up to 16, but I can let the registrar have a look. There is no number anywhere. I'm going to ask about these facts that I shall be citing from here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, but the witness should have the opportunity of seeing what it is you're reading from. Can we get a transcript --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think I have an English transcript of what it is the accused is referring to, but unless I can hear his first citation, or quotation, I can't really get us on track, but then I probably can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It's important that the witness also gets on track.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's the 5th of July, 1996. Let me first of all check that we're on the same document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. That's right. And then, number 1, it says Mr. Harmon: Our next witness is Mr. Erdemovic. And then it says Drazen Erdemovic called. And then further on he takes the solemn declaration, and then on the next page some questions are put to him. I'm not going to dwell on all of that now. The question:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Erdemovic, on the 10th of July did your detachment receive orders to take part in an action of the Bosnian Serbs against Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of orders did you receive?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: We came to the military barracks for our regular duties, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness -- do we have a copy in B/C/S for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. There is copy in B/C/S I think being handed to the witness now. I haven't yet found the reference to the 10th of -- yes, I have. I've found that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What page is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's about three different page numbers. It's page 26, but this is reverse page numbering. I can simply lay this on the overhead projector, if that will help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may not. You referred to the 5th of July, 1996. The date of the hearing I have is the 22nd of May, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. This one is, I think, the sentencing hearing, or a hearing, and it's the 5th of July, 1996. And I have it without -- it's a filing and it comes without ERN page numbers, but it does have filing page numbers which run reverse order, starting at page 29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we're simply wasting time. Let's go on with the questions and we'll see how we get on. Yes, Mr. Milosevic, what is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm just going to quote this. The question says:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go back a bit. Did you receive orders in relation to what you were supposed to do with the civilians that you find in Srebrenica? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Answer. This is your answer:

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: We were told explicitly not to touch the civilians. Is that right, Mr. Erdemovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who said that to you? And then your answer is:

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Milorad Pelemis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were these orders taken out vis-a-vis this person who was 30 years old?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No. This Lieutenant Pelemis ordered a man to kill this man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who gave this order? Who was this order given to? And then you say that this man's name was Zoran. However, the question pertains to what is on the page -- on this page, a bit earlier on. You spoke about it earlier today as well. You said that you saw about 200 civilians when you came to town, is that right, and that these were mostly elderly people?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I said today, and I've always said all along, that we came across some civilians, and we told them to walk in front of us so that they would not get killed and that we would take them to the football stadium because that's what we were told to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I did not hear that and perhaps it was misinterpreted here that you said that there were about 200 of them. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He did say that. That's my recollection.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right. Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So please, I'm very much interested in this, because you showed a picture here of General Mladic. And anybody can recognise him, by the way. Further on, on the next page of this transcript, you say: "Later on that same morning, Mr. Erdemovic, did you have occasion to see General Mladic in Srebrenica?" Or, rather, this is the question that is being put to you. I'm reading the transcript. Your answer:

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I received orders from the commander to go back to the beginning of town where we had entered it and that I should wait there, myself and two friends. When General Mladic passes there, I'm supposed to report to Mr. Pelemis to say that he had passed there. That's what I did when General Mladic passed there. So your commander dispatched you to the entrance into the town just to let him know whether General Mladic had passed there or not; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No, that's not right. I said that our commander sent us to establish a checkpoint at the other end of town from where we entered town and we should stay there and we should let him know when General Mladic passes there in order to provide security for that part of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because I wish to clarify this and that is why I'm reading the transcript, because it says here: I received orders to go back to the entrance where we had entered and to let Lieutenant Pelemis know when General Mladic passes there that he did pass, and that is indeed what I did when General Mladic passed there. That is to say, we let them know that he had passed. And then you were asked: Did Lieutenant Pelemis talk to Mladic or did he do anything else in relation to General Mladic? And your answer is: I really don't know because I was not present when they met, and I don't know whether they met at all. Is that right? Is that the way you put it there?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in relation to Mladic, you were just supposed to let your commander know that he had passed there. You do not know whether they met at all; is that right? That's what is written here.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. That's what I said all along.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then on the same page he asks you: Mr. Erdemovic, I would now like to draw your attention to the 16th of July and ask you whether you and other soldiers received orders to take part in a special assignment. Answer. You say: I was not personally told of any such instructions but the commander of the group had probably received some kind of orders with regard to this assignment. And then you say that you received orders from Brane Grujic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No, not Brane Grujic, Brano Gojkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise to Brane Grujic if there is a person by that name. There are many persons who have similar names. And tell me now, when did this start on the Pilica farm on the 16th of July? At what time? When did the first buses come, according to your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I could tell, I don't know. I don't even remember whether I had a watch, and I wasn't looking at any watch. It could have been in the morning between 10.00 and 11.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between 10.00 and 11.00.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you kept killing until the afternoon, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to me personally or us?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You personally and the remaining seven that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, until the men from Bratunac came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that the men from Bratunac came only after 2.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from 1000 to 1400 hours you were doing the killing. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now I'm interested in something else. This is on page 12 of what I have here as the transcript, the one that I've been quoting from. It says: "What was the position the other members who took part in the killing?" And you say: "Well, the position of individual members was almost like my own, that this should not be done. Well, I don't know. And some were doing it with a kind of vengeance." And then you're further asked whether you can say a bit more about it. Answer, you say: "This was a man who allegedly was saying that he said that the Bosnian Muslims had killed his brother who was 17 years old, and he said that he killed, that he wanted revenge, and that on that day he killed 250 of those Muslims from Srebrenica." Well, tell me now, this is what you said, what this transcript says, what I quoted from. And I have quoted your words verbatim. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you did not mention -- you did not mention that among you in that group of yours, the group of seven, there was anyone from Srebrenica whose brother had been killed by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: This person was not from Srebrenica. He was from Bosanska Krajina, from somewhere in Bosanska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was a member of your unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was killing out of revenge, according to what you've said here.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did somebody perhaps give him orders to kill out of revenge?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot think for him. I cannot know what went through his head at the time. That's what he was saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If you were ordered to do that, how does that fit in? You say that this man was saying that he was killing out of revenge because his brother had been killed by them. Make up your mind. What was the reason for doing such a senseless thing? Do you have any explanation?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I have no explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the suggestion that the witness is in some way being inconsistent in his answers is wholly unsupported by the questions put and really unfair. I'm not sure if you've got the passage Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that he's quoting from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We don't have the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have the transcript. I have one copy of it and I managed to find it. Can I at least place this passage on the overhead projector or hand it up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. If that could go on the overhead projector, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can see how it was that the witness came to give the answers that the accused is relying on. "What was the attitude of other members of your particular unit who participated in the executions?" led to the answer, "Well, the attitude of individual members was almost like mine, that this should not be done. I do not know. Whereas individuals did what they did with some kind of revenge." Asked if there were those who boasted, he said there were. "Can you expand?" He then gave the account of the person who said that the Bosnian Muslims had killed his brother who was 17. That's the way it emerged and there is no question of any inconsistency on the part of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. That can come back, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's exactly what I had quoted. I was only quoting from the transcript. The reply reads literally: "There was man who allegedly said -- that is what he said, that allegedly Bosnian Muslims had killed his brother who was 17, and he said that he had killed, that he wanted to take his revenge, and that on that day he had killed 250 Muslims from Srebrenica."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we have the point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is a quotation from that passage, and I was asking the witness about this statement of his.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm switching the microphone off. We have the point. We've heard both sides. We're going to adjourn now. Before we do, I'm going to give a short ruling in relation to the next witness, Colm Doyle. We have a motion for part of his statement to be admitted under Rule 92 bis. We will admit that part. The witness will in fact be giving evidence live on the most substantial parts of his evidence and he will be available for cross-examination. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Would you like the other transcript copied and available after the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'd better have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I'm helpfully reminded that the motion for consideration of the plea agreement was a document under seal in another Chamber. Now, the plea agreement itself, it may be the motion's been provided to the accused under Rule 68. I'll check on whether steps were taken with that other Chamber. That was certainly the position at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. You've got 50 minutes left if you want it, if you require it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I think you should give me more time, because I quite clearly cannot complete my cross-examination by the end of the day today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You must finish by the end of the day today because the witness cannot be here for longer. But let's get on with it now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, I must protest categorically, because this is a witness who according to his own admission killed more than a hundred people. He is attributing this to various backgrounds, and there's not enough time for him to be cross-examined. He cannot remain. I can't understand that explanation, and I don't think the public will either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have heard the ruling. It takes account of his evidence. Now, so far you haven't challenged very much of it. That is the crucial point, not the witness's background but how much of his evidence that you actually challenge. So far there's been very little. So 50 minutes should be more than adequate. But let's not waste time by discussing it further.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that it is quite clear to you and to everybody else that neither Serbia nor I have anything to do with these events in Srebrenica, Mr. May. But if that is not challenging the testimony, then that's up to you, as everything else is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Erdemovic, under whose command was your 10th Sabotage Detachment?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Under the command of the Main Staff, the department for security and safety and intelligence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, did anyone from that department or from the Main Staff order you to kill those people?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I said earlier on, and I will repeat, I personally was ordered to do it by Brano Gojkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you mentioned an unknown lieutenant colonel who gave such orders to Brano Gojkovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I am saying as far as I'm concerned who gave me the order, but I do also know that this lieutenant colonel couldn't give me -- us such an order if Pelemis had not allowed it or somebody from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand Pelemis was a commander of your detachment. He was not from the Main Staff. Are you saying that a lieutenant colonel that you don't know was a mediator between Pelemis and his unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who this lieutenant colonel was, whether he was a mediator or whether he asked our unit or anything like that. I can't explain that because I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you -- have you heard of Jugoslav Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I heard of Jugoslav Petrusic while I was in the prison here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you hear about him?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I read this in the newspapers, in the Vesti from Belgrade, that he and Pelemis and certain individuals from my unit were in Zaire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about what they did in Zaire?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything except what I read in the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you believe that the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska had sent them to Zaire?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that, and I don't believe it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But since you were a member of the army of Republika Srpska, as you claim, I assume that you must have been aware of orders coming from the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska in connection with the events of which you were a participant. Let me read to you that on the 9th of July, 1995, there's an urgent telegram. It has been registered under the 9th of July, et cetera, to the president of Republika Srpska for his information to the command -- forward command post of the Drina Corps, General Gvero, General Krstic, and the command of the Drina Corps around -- regarding combat activities around Srebrenica. And it says: "The president of Republika Srpska has been informed that units are successfully carrying out operations around Srebrenica and that they have achieved results, putting them in a position to be able to capture the town of Srebrenica itself." So this is dated the 9th of July. "The president of the republic is satisfied with the results of the combat activities around Srebrenica and agrees that those activities be continued to take control of Srebrenica, disarm Muslim terrorist bands, and totally demilitarise the Srebrenica enclave. The president of the Republika Srpska has ordered that in continuation of combat operations, full protection be provided to members of UNPROFOR and the Muslim civilian population and that their security be guaranteed if they cross into the territory of Republika Srpska pursuant to the order of the president of Republika Srpska, issue orders to all combat units participating in combat operations around Srebrenica to provide maximum protection and security for all members of UNPROFOR and the civilian Muslim population. "Order subordinate units to refrain from destruction of civilian targets unless they are forced to do so due to strong resistance by the enemy, prohibit the torching of housing facilities, and treat the civilian population and prisoners of war in accordance with the Geneva Conventions of the 12th of August, 1949." Signed by the assistant of the commander of the Main Staff, Major General Zdravko Tolimir. So this order says that all subordinate units must be informed of these instructions. Were such instructions given to you or were you informed about them, the instructions of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I said during the examination-in-chief that Pelemis said that we mustn't shoot civilians and that civilians should be advised to go to the football stadium in Srebrenica. That is what I was told.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were not conveyed verbatim this order that arrived on the 9th of July during the fighting around Srebrenica and when there was an indication that the town could be captured?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about what you just read out.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be exhibited, please, Mr. May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let the Prosecution see this document. Have you -- having heard it read out do you have any objection or would you like to have a look at it first?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have a look at it first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd hand it to the Prosecution, please. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a stamp and the number under which it is registered. You can see that in the rectangular stamp, that it was received and registered under a certain number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Erdemovic, to follow on to this question, I gather that your answer was that this order was not conveyed to you or it was not shown to you apart from what Petrusic told you, that civilians should not be killed.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: The order that you read was not conveyed to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the decision of the president of the Republika Srpska taken on the 11th of July, 1995? I leave out the preamble which refers to a certain paragraph of the constitution of Republika Srpska. It is the decision on the appointment of a civilian commissioner for the municipality of Serbian Srebrenica. I will leave out parts that are not of significance. There is reference to providing conditions for the efficient functioning of the authorities. In point 3, it says: "In cooperation with the Ministry of the Interior, set up a public security station, the prime task of which is to protect the personal and public property of citizens and prevent any criminal activity." Point 4: "The commissioner will make sure that the civilian and military bodies --" that all prisoners, all people who took part in combat against the forces of Republika Srpska should be treated as prisoners of war. The decisions of the commissioner are binding for all organs of authority in Srebrenica municipality. So those who took part in battles to be treated as prisoners of war, and the civilian population has the right to choose where it will reside, whether it will stay on or move out. Are you aware of this decision taken on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this also be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Show it to the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know where these particular documents come from. The versions being produced I don't think come from us. If we can track them down as documents coming from us then there will be no problem at all about allowing them to be produced other than simply being marked for identification, otherwise, I would be grateful to know where the origin is, but I'm looking into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. What is the source of these documents, please, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The source of these documents, Mr. May, is the archives of Republika Srpska. All those documents were published as a collector of documents, that is containing orders from the wartime period, orders issued at various levels of Republika Srpska. And this one obviously has to do with the question of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. The simplest course may be this, that we will mark them for identification while the Prosecution make their investigations, and we will begin with the first one, which I will hand to the registrar now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the telegram dated the 9th of July, 1995, will be marked for identification as Defence Exhibit 171. Your Honour, the second decision, dated the 11th of July, 1995, will be marked for identification as Defence Exhibit 172.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Erdemovic, regarding your own unit and some other units that you were asked about by Mr. Nice, you mentioned the Panthers, Crni, and some other units, and you say that they were -- that there were members of the Bijeljina corps, there were some refugees from the environs of Tuzla. They wore red and green berets, et cetera. And in answer to a question by Mr. Nice who gave them orders, you answered that you assumed that they received them from the Main Staff; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what basis do you assume that you -- your unit received orders from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't assume that my unit received directives from the Main Staff; I know that my unit received directives from them. I know that for certain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of what?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Because I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since I assume you know, I'm asking you on what basis you know.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Because we were a unit that belonged to the security service attached to the Main Staff, and I know that all orders that reached us came from the intelligence officer whose name was Petar Salapura.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nice asked you whether you had any knowledge regarding the links between your 10th Sabotage Detachment and the French intelligence service, and you said you had none; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who sent those men from the 10th Sabotage Detachment to Zaire?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I can't answer that question because I learnt about it while I was in prison here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many men in all were there in the 10th Sabotage Detachment? The number probably varied, but let's say during the time period you're testifying about, how many men did it number?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Between 50 and 60 persons, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive a salary?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: We did. Sometimes we didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your salary?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not even roughly?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Not even roughly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Quite incredible that you can't even remember how big your salary was.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: It's not quite incredible. I can't remember, and I don't want to say something and I don't want it to turn out later on that I said something that was wrong. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the fact that you were given the assignment to see when General Mladic would pass, doesn't that show that General Mladic had nothing to do with your detachment?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, have you ever heard of Philippe Rondeau or Patrick Foret? Have you ever heard these names?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to Pelemis, have you heard of a certain Avdo and Amir, nicknamed Brada, from Tuzla? Alija Amerhodzic from Tuzla? Have you heard of them?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of that unit of yours having had some kind of a company that was involved in arms trade and that it was even registered in Sofia in Bulgaria? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Do you know anything about a base of that unit of yours in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that we did carry out some tasks in the territory of Doboj and that mountain there, I've forgotten its name -- Ozren. I think that there were intelligence people out there, and we went to see them when we were given such tasks, and they were supposed to give us information. I know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of tasks were you given?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: We would go behind the positions of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do behind the positions of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Reconnoiter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just reconnoiter?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: We reconnoitered. Once we were supposed to destroy a bridge that was on the Krivaja river. That's what I know. That's where I was. And I don't know what else took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name Branko Vlaco?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Explain. In connection with what?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Quite a few times he came from Serbia with Pelemis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was he in contact with?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, with Pelemis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know of a certain Mihajl Vandrain [phoen], also known as Michel?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've never heard of him?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, could we just briefly have a look at a few clips from a tape that I gave your technical people here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know Savanovic, don't you? You mentioned him among the persons who took part.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The legal officer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few brief clips from a particular tape. And I'd like to put questions to the witness about it subsequently. I can barely see a thing, and there doesn't seem to be any sound either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this Savanovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't see a thing in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: See if you lean forward. If you lean forward, Mr. Erdemovic, see if you can see anything. You might be able to see a bit more. It's very difficult.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer is no, this is not Savanovic. I don't know, I've never seen the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You say that you've never seen this man?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we get a better copy of this tape, we'll have a look, but it is claimed here that the massacre was agreed upon because it was the end of the war and that was the way in which Serbs could be accused of genocide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We don't know who the man is. The witness doesn't recognise him. So what you have there is certainly not evidence. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that units of Naser Oric, a few days before Srebrenica was taken, left Srebrenica altogether?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not know that all units had left. But later on I heard that Naser Oric was not in Srebrenica and that his non-commissioned officers and commissioned officers weren't there either, that they were at a meeting in Tuzla. Now, how correct this is I cannot say, but I could see that in Srebrenica there was no resistance so I think there was no military in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when Naser Oric left Srebrenica with his army?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about some kind of agreement being reached concerning his departure from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you were in the area at the time and since this has to do with the activity of your 10th Sabotage Detachment, have you ever heard of a meeting between General Morillon and some other representatives of anybody, the Muslims or your 10th Sabotage Detachment, before the attack in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And do you know that on the 10th of July, 1995, in Zvornik, in the house of the former president of the municipality, a Muslim, a meeting was held with some representatives of the Muslim government and that General Janvier was there, that it was being discussed there that Srebrenica could fall without any fighting and that French and Belgium units could withdraw before that and that the corridor should be opened for the withdrawal of Naser Oric's forces, and also that some money was mentioned that was supposed to be paid to your detachment for doing this dirty work?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about any kind of money or gold and things like that?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I did hear about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that afterwards, Pelemis and individuals from Vlasenica shared some money and that they found some gold. Now, whether that's true or something, I don't know, but I heard about this while I was still at the military medical hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did they get this money from that you say they shared?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want to remind you that you said to the journalist of ABC news, Vanesa Vasic-Janekovic, a statement that the massacre in Pilica took place on account of money, and you even said that somebody promised Pelemis 12 kilogrammes of gold for carrying out this massacre in Pilica.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I said -- I said what I said to you just now, that I heard that later, while I was in hospital. I don't know this exactly, that I heard all of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have this here, ERN 0305056, but I'm not going to quote that. I'm going to quote page 8. I'm going to read something from page 8. It's a statement made here. Vanesa Vasic-Janekovic was a witness here on the 8th of March, 1996, and she made this statement to Peter Nicholson. She said that she asked Erdemovic about his past service, about his past in general, his activities. He also showed her his contract that was videotaped, together with his military ID and documents from the hospital. This is on page 8. And then also she says that somebody explained that somebody had promised Pelemis 12 kilogrammes of gold for the massacre in Pilica an that Pelemis was aware of this promise before the massacre had taken place. And at the end of the paragraph it says that Erdemovic and Kremenovic said that from a jeweller in Bijeljina they heard that Pelemis had ordered a thick gold chain of the best quality with very valuable workmanship. So let me skip a paragraph now. It says Kremenovic said Salapura communicated directly with General Mladic but he acted as if he did not have to receive any orders from him because from time to time, he became -- he behaved as if he were his equal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let the witness answer these various allegations. Did you meet this particular journalist? Do you remember that, Mr. Erdemovic, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did you say that Pelemis -- or it had been explained that somebody had promised Pelemis gold for the massacre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's what I heard when I was in hospital. I did not know that before. I heard all of these things when I got out of hospital, and I heard that it was correct that some -- that somebody said that Pelemis had commissioned such a chain from jeweller Marjanovic. That's why I thought that it was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just show you something. It is ERN -- I can't really find my way. This is page 00866 -- 86028. I can't really read the last number. I guess it's a 9. It's quite illegible. You say -- Where did you hear about the killing in Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: In Bijeljina. Well, it will be heard at the VMA. At the VMA I heard about this. My wife heard about it when she came to visit me, that Pelemis, Franc Kos, and this Brano, and I don't know who else, because of some kind of gold, that people were killed because of that gold, because of this money, because of all of that. All of that was heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when did you first hear anything about killings in Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. In hospital, a few days later. I was wounded. I came to hospital and my wife came and she mentioned some 100.000 marks. My wife, when she travelled to Belgrade, travelled with the lover of Milorad Pelemis. I didn't know about that. And this lover said that they had a good time together. Milorad Pelemis's friends from Vlasenica, that they were having a good time in Belgrade and -- in Belgrade hotels and that they bought cars, and that's how I came to this conclusion. And my wife can confirm that she heard about the gold. So what do you know about, this Mr. Erdemovic? Did these people -- were these people killed because the perpetrators were paid to commit this massacre?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how to answer that question. I wasn't paid at all, but the persons that I mentioned, I heard that they had done all that, and that is probably all true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they received the money, and they were your superiors, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Pelemis and certain individuals from Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you told Vanesa Janekovic that Salapura behaved as if he didn't have to follow orders from Mladic -- is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that to Vanesa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just quoted what Kremenovic said, and this is on page 8 of this translation of Vanessa. 03052963 is the page number. That he was acting as if he didn't have to follow orders from him as he behaved as if they were equals. And you heard that Salapura would do whatever he wanted.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes Kremenovic said that. I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is Vanessa's statement, Vanesa Janekovic's statement. Vlasic Janekovic. Very well. When your wife came to the Military Medical Academy hospital, you heard that the killings were done for money; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't say that I heard that people were killed for money, nor did my wife say that. She just said that they used some gold to have a good time in Belgrade hotels and shop around. They didn't know -- she didn't know about the killings at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As for Stanko Savanovic's statement in connection with the events in Srebrenica, apparently there were contacts with French officers in Zvornik where there was an arrangement made about the surrender of Srebrenica. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you yourself said that you received explicit orders not to hurt civilians; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We received such an order on the 11th in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your commander Pelemis; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know anything at all about a letter sent by Naser Oric to Alija Izetbegovic after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know nothing about it, about the agreement to surrender Srebrenica and the money he received?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And do you remember that in 1995 French pilots were captured? Do you remember those pilots?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I saw that on television, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the role of members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment in concealing those pilots and hiding them even from General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there a camp of the 10th Sabotage Detachment in Dragosevac near Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is where the Vlasenica platoon was quartered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then these captured French pilots were apparently concealed in that camp.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I hear that for the first time today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know anything about them being hidden away even from the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that any one of the participants in this crime in Srebrenica was held accountable or investigations conducted against them or put on trial or searched for, except for you?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't answer that question. I'm not the person to decide who would be tried, investigated, or where or when.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doesn't it seem to be rather strange that only you who was arrested by the Yugoslav --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not for the witness to answer that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I will prove - I don't have to do that through this witness - what is the background of this and that the French and other intelligence services were involved and that the perpetrators of the crime were promised --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll hear all about your evidence in due course, but let's finish this witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't complete my cross-examination of this witness, but of course it is up to you when you decide to interrupt me, you will do so. I'm quite sure of that. Tell me, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic has a point. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps you really could consider the possibility of providing some additional time to Mr. Slobodan Milosevic to complete his cross-examination of this witness. I really do not understand the position of the Prosecution for such witnesses who are very important, and this has happened before. But the witness before you has made at least 13 statements that I have reviewed, at least 13 in connection with all these problems, and he participated in a number of trials here, including his own, and I don't see why he should be protected again when he is testifying before you. So I appeal to you to give this matter some thought. Perhaps some additional time could be given for the cross-examination of this witness. I understand that he has a problem with his job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll sit until 2.00, and we will then review the position. It depends what time -- use you make of your time, Mr. Milosevic, providing it's not wasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name Radinko Gajic?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Radinko Gajic from Kladanj. You don't know him?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Branko Vlaco. You know him. Yes?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Milorad Pelemis, you also know him.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Rade Petrovic from Srebrenica? A false passport.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know him. I read his name in the newspapers, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who do you know among the members of your 10th Sabotage Detachment that were engaged in Zaire?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember all the names that I read in the papers then. I know Pelemis. I know about -- you just mentioned the name, I've already forgotten it. Jugoslav Petrusic. I knew that they were men from our unit because I saw their pictures in the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have here -- since you say you saw pictures in the newspapers, I have a letter addressed to Colonel -- to a colonel, written by hand, from the Ministry of the Interior of France, and it begins with the words "Mon Colonel, The situation in your country is developing quickly." The date is the 7th of February, 1996. "And it is creating turbulence which are fatal for discretion and security linked to our service. Our common plan of cooperation has certainly not been neglected. On the contrary, the evolution of the Muslim factors in Bosnia retains our full attention in spite of TPI and the slanders that are appearing on a daily basis. You're welcome to Paris and we can guarantee safe sojourn if you are given permission to meet with us. Note, Jugo will give you all additional information." Signature illegible, note of the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Who is this letter written to, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, obviously to Jugoslav Petrusic, who was the liaison with the French service, and he's the one who should provide all the information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness knows nothing about this -- witness -- wait a moment. Don't interrupt, please. We'll have to consider carefully whether there's any relevance in these letters you're producing. Let us see the letter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here you are. I think that in the ministry in Paris, if you were to give such instructions, all this could be cleared up. I have already requested that the services who are assisting the side opposite should provide information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the relevance of all this? We've got -- let me just summarise what we have. We don't have an addressee for it, it's just described as Colonel. It's dated the 7th of February, 1996. At the moment, I can't see any relevance at all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Hand this back to the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall do my best to make relevance obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the company DAO Link [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then, I won't show you these bills. I shall keep them for another occasion, together with this letter. Do you know anything at all in connection with the name of Steve Hanke, for instance? Have you heard of that name?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You haven't heard of that name either. Very well. Have you heard of Richard Butler who was an American military analyst and whom the US government lent to this institution here?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I don't have to give this to you. ERO 876762. There's a conversation with Butler in which he says: "I have to point out that in 1995, with respect to Srebrenica, there were no activities of paramilitary formations. All the formations that were involved in the Srebrenica operation were under the command of the army and government of Republika Srpska. We didn't see any units out of their control." And then the Prosecutor -- it says here the Prosecutor. This is -- this was extracted from some newspapers by Mr. Nice or his associates, but obviously it's a transcript of your interview here. The Prosecutor: You reviewed many statements in connection with this case and some witnesses mention Arkan's Tigers and other paramilitaries who were particularly infamous in 1993 and 1994.
